title: Learning a Foreign Language
summary: Josh and Chuck explore how people learn a first language (L1) and second language (L2). They cover language acquisition theories: the critical period hypothesis (Wilder Penfield and Lamar Roberts, 1959), sponge theory, behaviorism (B.F. Skinner), and nativism (Noam Chomsky's universal grammar and language acquisition device). They discuss why children learn languages more easily than adults, the role of inhibitory neurons, brain language areas (Broca's area, Wernicke's area, angular gyrus) and Wernicke's aphasia, bilingual children, polyglots, and practical tips for adult learners such as immersion, input and output, vocabulary, short lessons, non-threatening environments, and mimicking sounds. They also cover reported cognitive, empathy, and Alzheimer's-delay benefits of bilingualism. The episode ends with listener mail about the pronunciation of "Steve Dor" (a trucker's correction).

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts open with chatter about Rick Allen of Def Leppard playing drums after losing an arm, then transition to the topic of learning foreign languages.

segments.title: Speaking multiple languages and personal language backgrounds
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the prestige of speaking several languages and share their own language backgrounds, including Josh's German study and his interest in learning Spanish.

segments.title: L1 acquisition introduction
segments.summary: Josh introduces first language (L1) acquisition as the natural process of learning to talk as a baby, and the hosts discuss reading ages.

segments.title: Critical period hypothesis
segments.summary: Josh describes the critical period hypothesis proposed by Wilder Penfield and Lamar Roberts in 1959, and the hosts compare it to the older idea that neurons were fixed at birth.

segments.title: Sponge theory
segments.summary: The sponge theory, that children absorb language passively, is described and criticized for underestimating active learning, with an analogy about a sponge beside a bucket of water.

segments.title: Behaviorism
segments.summary: B.F. Skinner's view that language is learned through reinforcement and punishment is explained, and the hosts note partial truth in competing theories.

segments.title: Nativism and universal grammar
segments.summary: Nativism is presented as the opposite of behaviorism, holding that humans are born with innate language abilities such as universal grammar, a cornerstone of Noam Chomsky's work.

segments.title: Phonemes and infant babbling
segments.summary: A language has roughly forty phonemes, and babies begin to grasp the relevant ones around six months, with babbling differing by language community.

segments.title: L2 acquisition and multilingual kids
segments.summary: Children learn second languages more easily than adults. Bilingual children do not fall behind, and the hosts discuss the upper limit of languages children can learn, plus famous multilingual people.

segments.title: Practice time and multilingual record holders
segments.summary: Linguists suggest spending twenty to thirty percent of waking time practicing a language, and multilingual figures are named, including a Canadian with 42 languages and a record holder at 59.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Critical period and inhibitory neurons
segments.summary: The hosts revisit the critical period, adult versus child learning, and why inhibitory neurons may make new languages harder to acquire by settling existing neural pathways. Adults outperform children on some measures, but children reach richer language understanding.

segments.title: Inhibitory neurons and Alzheimer's disease
segments.summary: Chuck describes research linking loss of inhibitory neurons to hyperactivity in the hippocampus in Alzheimer's disease, and the role of basket neurons.

segments.title: Brain language areas and aphasia
segments.summary: Broca's area, Wernicke's area, and the angular gyrus are described. Wernicke's aphasia is explained with an example, and the hosts share an anecdote about a relative's stroke.

segments.title: Brain hemispheres and language in children
segments.summary: Language areas are mostly in the left hemisphere in adults, while fMRI scans show both hemispheres active in children learning language.

segments.title: Developmental milestones and innate language ability
segments.summary: Predictable language milestones in children suggest an innate ability to learn language, and the hosts debate whether this supports nativism or behaviorism.

segments.title: Vocabulary growth
segments.summary: Vocabulary keeps growing past age eight, and the hosts discuss how hard it is to define words for children.

segments.title: Tips for adult language learners
segments.summary: Adults can learn a second language more slowly, requiring effort. Tips include immersion, input and output, vocabulary memorization, short manageable lessons, and a non-threatening environment with children's stories instead of grammar drills.

segments.title: Foreigner talk and mimicking sounds
segments.summary: Foreigner talk is described as slowed, simplified speech used by native speakers. Imitating sounds helps learners, and Josh shares his German pronunciation experience and his mother's imitation of British accents.

segments.title: Benefits of bilingualism
segments.summary: Hosts discuss reported benefits of learning languages, including empathy, conflict management, problem solving, cognitive tests, and delayed Alzheimer's onset by about five years, while questioning some studies.

segments.title: Listener mail: Steve Dor pronunciation
segments.summary: A listener who is a trucker writes in to settle a dispute about how 'Steve Dor' is pronounced, saying it is Steve Door, and both hosts respond.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck thanks the listener and gives the show's email address, and Josh closes with the iHeartRadio app reference.
